ideas.hypothesis: Recent eligibility persistence improving relative to longer eligibility memory, after stabilization, predicts stronger cross-sectional continuation.
Repeated eligibility flipping creates an exhaustion state whose stabilization may matter more than entry itself.
Re-entry after prior durable eligibility differs from first sustained entry because prior market-access memory persists.
Acceleration in eligibility persistence, not raw entry age, identifies maturation.
Cross-sectional breadth of stable requalifications may govern cash deployment.
Eligibility improvement without price confirmation may mean temporary universe churn rather than durable access.
Dispersion in eligibility-memory states identifies structural universe rotation.
A tiny causal survival model of continued eligibility may contain information beyond entry age.
Upward cross-sectional migration in eligibility memory may lead price leadership.
Aggregate requalification instability may be a cash/risk state rather than an asset selector.
